beginner: Chives are not fussy about soil and grow in almost any kind, but they do best in loose, fertile ground with some compost mixed in, kept evenly moist but never soggy. Good drainage matters most: an established clump handles a short dry spell, but ground that stays wet through winter can rot the roots and crown.
seasoned: Chives tolerate a wide range of soils but grow best in a well-drained loam rich in organic matter, kept evenly moist. The University of Minnesota recommends well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and Michigan State notes chives grow best in soils high in organic matter while adapting to most soil types. Work compost into the bed before planting to feed a clump you cut from for years, and site it where water does not stand, since a waterlogged crown, especially over winter, invites rot on this otherwise trouble-free perennial.

beginner: Chives grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, the range the University of Minnesota and Michigan State both list as best for chives; they still do fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Chives are not pH-sensitive, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Chives do not need much feeding. Mix some compost into the soil before planting, and that is often enough. If a clump looks weak or you cut it hard, give it a light feeding to bring back fresh green leaves. In a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out.
seasoned: Chives are light feeders with low nutrient needs and rarely need regular fertilizer. The University of Minnesota suggests only a very light application of a 5-10-5 fertilizer once each spring if a clump looks weak, on top of compost worked in before planting. A clump you cut from repeatedly benefits from a light feeding after a hard shearing to push fresh tender regrowth; in containers, where frequent watering leaches nutrients, a dilute liquid feed every four to six weeks keeps leaves green. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which softens the flavor.

beginner: Time to give your chives a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to give your chives a light feeding if they look weak.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-5, a little worked into the soil before planting, then feed lightly only if the plant looks weak or after you cut it hard.
seasoned: Light, balanced feeding for a low-demand perennial: a little 5-10-5 or balanced fertilizer worked in before planting, then an optional light feed in spring or after a hard cutting. Go easy on nitrogen, which softens flavor on a crop eaten fresh.

beginner: One light feeding in spring is plenty, or none at all if your soil is good; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every four to six weeks.
seasoned: A very light application of 5-10-5 once in spring is plenty for an established clump; a compost-rich bed often needs no feeding at all, with a light feed only after a hard shearing.

beginner: Tiny, slender pale-yellow to brown insects hiding down in the leaf folds, leaving silvery or whitish streaks and flecks on the green blades. Bad infestations make the foliage look bleached and papery.
seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) feeding in the leaf axils and folds, producing silvery-white stippling, streaking, and a bleached, papery look on heavy pressure; they favor hot, dry weather. On chives the damage is usually cosmetic, but a severe year degrades a leaf crop.

beginner: Thrips are minute sap-sucking insects, common on onion-family plants, that rasp the leaves and are worst in hot, dry weather. Chives usually shrug them off, but a heavy year can mark the leaves.
seasoned: Thrips tabaci, the principal allium thrips, rasps leaf surfaces and feeds on the sap; populations build fast in hot, dry conditions and on stressed plants.

beginner: Hose the plants down to knock thrips off, shear a badly streaked clump to the base so it regrows clean, and use insecticidal soap on the leaves if needed. Rinse cut leaves before use.
seasoned: Dislodge with a strong water jet, shear a heavily infested clump to the base to remove the population and force clean regrowth, and spray insecticidal soap or spinosad if warranted; conserve natural enemies (minute pirate bugs, lacewings). Keeping plants unstressed and watered blunts outbreaks.

beginner: Keep plants watered in hot spells, welcome helpful insects like lacewings and pirate bugs, and cut a marked-up clump back to force fresh leaves.
seasoned: Avoid drought stress, conserve natural enemies, cut back streaked foliage to reset the clump, and avoid siting chives beside heavily thrips-pressured onion or garlic plantings.

beginner: Rows of white dots punched down a leaf where the adult fly fed, then wavy pale mines inside the leaves, with small maggots or brown seed-like pupae tucked into the leaf bases. It shows up in spring and again in fall.
seasoned: Allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma): lines of white oviposition punctures down the distal leaf, followed by larval mines and brown puparia lodged in leaf sheaths and bulbs. The University of Maryland lists chive (A. schoenoprasum) among its hosts; wounds open the door to secondary bacterial and fungal rots.

beginner: The allium leafminer is a small fly whose larvae tunnel inside onion-family leaves, including chives, and burrow toward the base. It is a newer pest in parts of the eastern United States.
seasoned: Phytomyza gymnostoma, an invasive allium-specific fly with a spring flight (roughly March into May) and a fall flight (September into October); larvae mine toward the leaf base and bulb, with up to dozens of pupae per plant in severe cases.

beginner: Cover plants with floating row cover in early spring and again in fall to keep the flies off, cut off and destroy mined leaves, and clean up plant debris.
seasoned: Exclude the adults with floating row cover timed to the spring and fall flights, remove and destroy mined foliage, and sanitize crop debris; spinosad or azadirachtin can help where pressure is high. Rotation away from recently infested allium ground reduces carryover.

beginner: Use row cover during the spring and fall flights, remove mined leaves, and keep the bed clean.
seasoned: Row-cover through both flight periods, remove infested leaves, sanitize residue, and separate new plantings from pressured allium beds.

beginner: Yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth as small white maggots tunnel into the base of the plant and the bulbs below the soil, sometimes rotting the crown. Worst in cool, wet springs.
seasoned: Onion maggot (Delia antiqua) larvae mining into the basal plate, roots, and bulbs, causing wilting, yellowing, stunting, and crown rot; damage is worst in cool, moist springs and where allium debris accumulates. Established chive clumps are seldom destroyed but can be set back.

beginner: Onion maggots are the larvae of a fly that lays eggs at the base of onion-family plants; the maggots eat into the roots and bulbs. Chives are rarely hit hard, but a clump can be damaged.
seasoned: Delia antiqua overwinters as pupae in the soil; spring flies lay eggs at plant bases and successive generations attack roots and bulbs, favored by cool wet weather and by cull and debris that lure egg-laying.

beginner: There is no rescue for a maggot-riddled crown, so remove badly affected plants. Use row cover to keep the flies off, and clean up debris and culls that attract them.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infested plants, exclude flies with floating row cover, and sanitize debris and culls; rotation and avoiding dense allium plantings limit buildup. No effective organic rescue exists once larvae are in the crown.

beginner: Cover plants with row cover in spring, avoid leaving old bulbs and debris around, and do not crowd alliums together.
seasoned: Row-cover early, sanitize allium residue, rotate, and avoid clustering chives with other alliums that concentrate the fly.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the leaves and flower stalks, sometimes with sticky residue. Chives rarely get them badly, and their scent even helps keep aphids off nearby plants.
seasoned: Occasional aphid colonies on foliage and scapes; chives are among the most aphid-free herbs (their odor is credited with repelling aphids from neighbors), so infestations are minor and sporadic rather than a standing threat.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast on soft growth. They are an occasional, minor visitor on chives.
seasoned: Several aphid species may alight on chives in flushes of soft growth, but the plant's sulfur compounds make it an inhospitable host, so colonies rarely persist.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water or use insecticidal soap, and rinse cut leaves before use. It is seldom needed.
seasoned: A water jet or insecticidal soap handles the rare colony; conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and hoverflies, which the chive umbels also feed when in bloom.

beginner: Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check flower stalks now and then.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and monitor scapes; control is seldom warranted on chives.

beginner: Pale, fuzzy gray-violet patches on the leaves in cool, damp weather, with the blades yellowing and collapsing. It spreads fastest in wet, crowded, poorly drained plantings.
seasoned: Downy mildew (Peronospora destructor) producing pale oval patches that turn violet-gray with sporulation under moisture, with leaves paling, yellowing, and collapsing; it is favored by cool (below about 75°F), humid, wet conditions and affects chives among many alliums.

beginner: A fungus-like disease of the onion family, favored by cool, humid, wet conditions, that can affect chives along with onions, garlic, and leeks.
seasoned: Peronospora destructor, an oomycete spread by wind and splashing water and favored by cool, moist weather and long leaf-wetness periods; crowded, poorly drained plantings hold it.

beginner: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow by dividing crowded clumps, water at the base rather than over the leaves, and cut a badly hit clump back so it regrows in drier weather.
seasoned: Manage culturally: divide crowded clumps and space for airflow, irrigate at the soil line, remove infected foliage, and shear a heavily affected clump to regrow under drier conditions. The home garden has no reliable cure once it is established.

beginner: Space and divide plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and avoid soggy, shaded, crowded spots.
seasoned: Open the canopy by dividing, water at the base, site in well-drained sun, and avoid the cool, wet, crowded conditions the pathogen needs.

beginner: Bright orange raised spots or streaks (pustules) scattered on the leaves. Heavily rusted blades yellow and dry up. It is more common in wet seasons and on crowded, over-fed plants.
seasoned: Allium rust (Puccinia species) forming bright orange to rusty raised pustules on leaves and scapes, with chlorosis and dieback of heavily infected foliage; it is favored by moist conditions, crowding, and lush high-nitrogen growth, and affects chives along with garlic, leeks, and onions.

beginner: Rust is a fungal disease of the onion family, including chives, that shows as orange pustules on the leaves and spreads by airborne spores in damp weather.
seasoned: Puccinia rust fungi spread by airborne urediniospores in humid weather; dense stands and excess nitrogen worsen it.

beginner: Cut off and destroy rusty leaves or shear the clump to the base to regrow clean, thin crowded plantings for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and heavy nitrogen.
seasoned: Shear infected foliage (a hard cut to the base removes the pustules and regrows clean), divide to open crowded clumps, avoid overhead irrigation and heavy nitrogen, and remove debris. Fungicides are rarely warranted in a home planting.

beginner: Give plants room and airflow, water at the base, go easy on nitrogen, and remove rusty foliage promptly.
seasoned: Divide for airflow, moderate nitrogen, irrigate at the soil line, and cut out rust early before it spreads.

beginner: Yellowing, wilting plants whose roots and crown rot, with a fluffy white mold and tiny black specks (like poppy seeds) at the base. Affected plants do not recover, and the disease stays in the soil for many years.
seasoned: White rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) causing yellowing, wilting, and a soft rot of roots and crown, with a fluffy white mycelium and abundant tiny black sclerotia at the base; the sclerotia persist in soil for many years, and the disease affects chives with onions, garlic, and leeks.

beginner: White rot is a serious soil fungus of the onion family that rots the roots and crown. Once it is in the soil it lasts a very long time, so keeping it out is the whole game.
seasoned: Sclerotium cepivorum, a soilborne fungus favored by cool, moist soil; its long-lived sclerotia make an infested site unusable for alliums for a decade or more, so exclusion and sanitation are the only real controls.

beginner: There is no cure. Remove and destroy affected plants along with the soil around the roots, and do not plant chives, onions, or garlic in that spot again. Never move infected soil or plants to a clean bed.
seasoned: No rescue: rogue out affected plants with surrounding soil, avoid spreading infested soil on tools or transplants, and do not replant alliums in the site. Long rotation is the standing management.

beginner: Start with clean plants, do not bring in soil from an infected garden, and rotate onion-family plants to fresh ground.
seasoned: Plant clean, sclerotia-free stock, quarantine infested ground from alliums, sanitize tools, and never import garden soil of unknown history.

beginner: Small whitish sunken spots on the leaves in cool, wet weather that can run together and brown out the tops, sometimes with a gray fuzzy mold. It is worst in humid, crowded plantings.
seasoned: Botrytis leaf blight and neck rot (Botrytis species) producing small white sunken leaf spots that coalesce into blast and tip dieback under cool, moist conditions, sometimes with gray sporulation; humid, crowded stands favor it, and it affects chives among the alliums.

beginner: Botrytis is a gray-mold fungus of the onion family that spots and blights the leaves in cool, damp, crowded conditions.
seasoned: Botrytis fungi favored by cool, wet, humid weather and dense canopies; splashing water and leaf wetness spread the spores.

beginner: Remove spotted leaves or shear the clump to regrow, open up crowded plantings for airflow, and water at the base instead of over the leaves.
seasoned: Cull spotted foliage or shear the clump to regrow, divide to open the stand, irrigate at the soil line, and remove senescing debris. Fungicides are seldom needed on a home chive planting.

beginner: Space and divide for airflow, water at the soil line, and clean up dead foliage.
seasoned: Divide for airflow, water low and early, and sanitize dead foliage to cut inoculum.

beginner: Water about once a week so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week. Established chives handle a dry spell, but even water keeps the leaves tender.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; chives are drought tolerant once the clump is established, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and green over the long cutting season. Do not let established plants sit in constantly wet soil.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is hot and dry. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in hot, dry spells; the University of Minnesota advises watering deeply when rainfall is sparse so the soil does not dry out around the roots. A mulch helps hold even moisture for a clump you cut from for years.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks the leaf diseases (downy mildew, rust, botrytis) chives can catch in cool, wet, crowded conditions.

beginner: Leaves go yellow and floppy and the base can rot in soggy soil, especially over winter.
seasoned: Yellowing, floppy foliage and crown or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground, especially over winter; downy mildew and botrytis also flare in cool, saturated, crowded conditions.

beginner: Wilting leaves that taste sharper and tougher, and slowed growth when the soil dries out for too long.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tougher, sharper foliage in prolonged drought; established clumps recover quickly once watered, but a dry, hot spell can push them toward summer dormancy.

beginner: Chive seeds take 2 to 3 weeks to come up, so keep the soil surface evenly damp the whole time. Do not let it dry out while they are sprouting.
seasoned: Chive seed is slow, 2 to 3 weeks, so keep the surface evenly moist through the whole germination; letting it dry mid-sprout stalls an already slow stand.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while a new plant gets going. Water deeply in dry spells, and mulch to hold the moisture.
seasoned: Steady moisture matters most while a new clump puts its root system down; UMN advises watering deeply when rainfall is sparse so the soil does not dry around the roots. Mulch helps hold it for a clump you will cut from for years.

beginner: Established chives handle a dry spell, but even water, about an inch a week, keeps the leaves tender for cutting. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry, and know that a long hot drought makes them tough and can send them dormant early.
seasoned: Once the clump is established chives are drought tolerant, but steady moisture, about an inch a week, keeps the leaves tender and green over the long cutting season. Water at the soil line to keep the foliage dry against downy mildew, rust, and botrytis in crowded conditions. Prolonged drought toughens the leaves and can push the plant into early summer dormancy in hot regions.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while chives bloom. The flowers are edible, and steady water keeps the leaves tender if you keep snipping.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the bloom; the flowers are edible, and steady water holds leaf quality if you keep cutting alongside the blossoms.

beginner: Water little or none while chives are dormant. The main danger now is rot from soggy winter soil, so do not let the resting clump sit wet.
seasoned: Cut back watering as the clump goes dormant; the biggest risk now is crown and root rot from constantly wet, poorly drained ground over winter, so do not let a dormant clump sit in wet soil.

beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender; chives handle a short dry spell once established, but long droughts make them tough.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps chives growing tender and green; an established clump tolerates short dry spells, but prolonged drought toughens the leaves and can trigger early summer dormancy in hot regions.

beginner: Keep the soil moist while the seeds are sprouting, which takes a couple of weeks, and while a new plant gets going.
seasoned: Steady moisture matters most through the slow germination (2 to 3 weeks) and while a new clump establishes; once the root system is down the plant is forgiving.

beginner: The easiest way to start chives is to buy a small pot or split a clump from a friend, which is ready to cut almost right away. You can also grow them from seed, but the seed is slow, taking a couple of weeks or more, so start it indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, sowing a small pinch of seeds in each cell and growing them on as a little clump that you plant out whole without separating, or sow it outside once the soil is warm. Plant outside in spring in cold areas, or in fall through winter where summers are hot. Space plants about 8 to 12 inches apart, and remember one clump can be split into many.
seasoned: Chives are easiest to establish from a division or a nursery clump, which gives a cuttable plant in weeks, but they also grow readily from seed. The seed is slow, germinating over about 2 to 3 weeks (up to 4 to 6 in cool soil), so start it indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, sowing a pinch of about 8 to 10 seeds per cell and growing them on as an undivided clump that transplants out whole after hardening off, with no thinning (RHS), or direct-sow once the soil warms. Plant outdoors in spring after hard-frost danger passes in cold regions, or in fall through late winter in mild and hot regions. Set clumps 8 to 12 inches apart; they widen over the years and are the easiest herb to propagate by simply lifting and splitting an established clump.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix with some organic matter.

beginner: Mix in a little compost for steady nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost; chives are light feeders, so no heavy starter fertilizer is needed.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check every day or two in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture every day or two in warmth and water deeply before the mix dries out.

beginner: Feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every four to six weeks, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container chives need only a light feed, a dilute liquid fertilizer every four to six weeks, because frequent watering leaches the limited mix.

beginner: Chives are very hardy, so a pot can stay outside through fall and winter in most areas; the leaves die back and the plant regrows in spring. In the coldest zones the small amount of soil in a pot freezes harder than the ground, so sink the pot in the garden, move it against the house, or mulch it heavily. You can also dig up a small clump in fall, pot it, and grow it on a bright windowsill for winter snipping.
seasoned: Chives are frost-hardy to roughly zone 3 and go dormant over winter, so an outdoor pot simply dies back and returns in spring. Container root volume freezes harder than open ground, so in cold zones sink the pot, cluster pots against a wall, or mulch to buffer the roots. A classic trick is to lift a small divided clump in fall, pot it, give it a few weeks of cold to satisfy dormancy, then bring it to a sunny window for fresh winter leaves.

beginner: Chives are one of the best herbs for a pot. Use a container at least 6 inches deep with drainage holes, keep it watered, and snip leaves as you need them. A pot does well on a sunny windowsill or step, and because chives are so hardy it can carry on outdoors long after tender herbs are done.
seasoned: Chives grow very well in a container at least 6 inches deep, harvested cut-and-come-again. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast, and feed only lightly. A pot is the easiest way to keep chives by the kitchen door, to move a small clump indoors for winter cutting, and to contain a plant that self-sows in the open garden.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps chives tender and productive.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits chives well, smoothing out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender over a long cutting season.

beginner: Chives have shallow roots, so a pot at least 6 inches deep is fine. Extra width lets the clump spread and gives you more to cut.
seasoned: Chives have a shallow, fibrous root system and do not need depth; a pot 6 inches or deeper is plenty, and extra width lets the clump widen and lets you grow more to cut from.

beginner: Do not plant chives where you recently grew onions, garlic, or leeks, since onion-family plants share soil diseases and pests that build up. Because chives stay put for years, this mainly matters when you first choose the spot.
seasoned: Avoid establishing chives where onions, garlic, leeks, shallots, or other chives grew recently: the alliums share soilborne troubles, above all white rot (whose sclerotia persist for years), plus pink root, onion maggot, and thrips. Because chives are a long-lived perennial planted once and left in place, rotation matters mainly when you first site a clump or replace an old one; keep new plantings out of recently cropped allium ground.

beginner: Chives are in the onion family, so they can pick up the same soil diseases as onions and garlic. Since a chive clump stays in one place for years, just choose a spot where you have not grown onion-family plants recently, ideally after leafy greens or beans. Chives that flower drop seed, so pull up stray seedlings where you do not want them.
seasoned: Chives are an allium, so they share the onion family's soilborne diseases (white rot, pink root) and pests (onion maggot, thrips, allium leafminer). Standard allium guidance keeps the family off the same ground for several years, but chives are a permanent perennial, so the practical rule is to establish a new clump in ground that has not recently grown onions, garlic, or leeks, and to follow a leafy or legume crop rather than another allium. A clump left to flower self-sows freely, so pull stray seedlings that come up out of place.

beginner: Chives are not like cilantro; flowering is normal and the flowers are pretty and edible. But two things happen when they bloom: the leaves get tougher, and if the flowers go to seed you get lots of surprise seedlings. So enjoy some flowers, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. That takes off the old flower stalks before they seed and brings back fresh, tender leaves.
seasoned: Chives do not bolt-and-quit the way lettuce or cilantro do; flowering is a normal, even desirable, part of a perennial allium's year. In late spring to early summer the clump sends up round pink to pale purple flower scapes above the leaves, and the flowers are edible and good for pollinators. The catch is twofold: the foliage around the scapes turns tougher and more hollow, and a clump left to set seed self-sows prolifically (garlic chives especially). The standard practice is to enjoy some flowers, then shear the whole clump down to about 1 to 2 inches after bloom, which removes the spent scapes before they seed and forces a fresh flush of tender leaves. Removing flower stalks at the soil line as they fade also prevents unwanted volunteer seedlings.

beginner: Chives flower in late spring or early summer with round pink-purple blooms, and that is normal, not a mistake. The flowers taste good and feed the bees. Just know the leaves get tougher around the flowers, and the seeds can sprout all over, so cutting the clump back after it blooms keeps the leaves tender and the plant tidy.
seasoned: Flowering in chives is a perennial life-cycle event in late spring to early summer, not a heat response, and it is partly a feature: the pink-purple umbels are edible and strong insectary plants. Its practical downside is coarsened, hollow foliage and prolific self-seeding, both fixed by shearing the clump hard after bloom to renew tender leaves and cut off seed set. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) flower later, in late summer, are white, and self-sow so freely they can become weedy if the scapes are not removed.

beginner: Do not leave cut chives out on the counter, where they wilt fast. Chill them and use them soon after cutting.
seasoned: Fresh chives wilt quickly at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; the leaves lose their delicate onion aroma fast once cut, so use them soon.

beginner: Store fresh chives unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where they keep about a week. Wash them only when you are ready to use them.
seasoned: Refrigerate fresh chives unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel, in the crisper; they hold about 1 week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Chives are best frozen rather than dried. Chop the clean leaves and freeze them loose or in an ice-cube tray with a little water, then use them straight from the freezer without thawing. Drying works but loses most of the flavor.
seasoned: Chives freeze better than they dry: snip the washed leaves and freeze them loose or in ice-cube trays with a little water; the University of Minnesota notes you can use the frozen pieces straight from the freezer without thawing. Drying is the weakest option, since dried chives lose most of their delicate flavor, so freezing is preferred for keeping.

beginner: The best way to store chives is to leave them growing and cut what you need. Picked chives keep about a week in the fridge. To save extra, freeze them chopped rather than drying them, since drying loses most of the flavor.
seasoned: Chives are best fresh, and because the clump keeps producing, the easiest storage is to cut what you need as you need it. Cut chives keep about a week refrigerated. For longer keeping, freeze them chopped (loose or in cubes) rather than drying, which sacrifices most of the flavor; frozen chives go straight into cooking without thawing.

beginner: There are really two kinds. Common chives have thin, hollow leaves and pink-purple flowers and taste mildly of onion; the named types just vary in how fine or sturdy the leaves are. Garlic chives are a different plant with flat leaves, a mild garlic taste, and white flowers in late summer, and they take heat well but spread by seed a lot. They all grow the same way, so pick by flavor and looks, and cut off the flowers if you do not want seedlings everywhere.
seasoned: Chives come in two distinct plants. Common chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are the familiar fine, hollow-leaved clump with pink-purple spring flowers and a mild onion taste; named selections differ mostly in leaf fineness and vigor, from the slender Fine Leaf and Grolau strains favored for pots and forcing, to the thick, easy-cutting Staro, to taller showy-flowered Forescate. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) are a separate species with flat leaves, a garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers; they are tougher in heat and drought but self-sow aggressively. All are grown much the same way, so choice comes down to flavor (onion versus garlic), leaf form, and how much you value the flowers, while any chive self-seeds if you let the blooms set seed.

beginner: Chives are a classic companion herb: their oniony scent is said to help keep aphids and some other pests off nearby plants, and their early flowers feed pollinators and helpful insects. Gardeners traditionally tuck them at the base of roses (for black spot and aphids) and apple trees (for scab), and near carrots and tomatoes. The one plant to keep them away from is beans and peas, which onion-family plants can slow down.
seasoned: Much of the chive companion tradition rests on two real mechanisms: allium sulfur compounds that deter aphids and some fungal problems, and the flowering umbels' pull on hoverflies, ladybugs, and parasitoid wasps. Michigan State, citing Penn State, passes along the traditional pairings of chives at the base of apple trees (to help suppress apple scab) and roses (black spot), plus a reputed boost to carrots. These are hedged tradition with a plausible mechanism, not measured trials. The one well-grounded caution is the allium-legume antagonism: onions and their relatives are widely documented to inhibit beans and peas, so keep chives away from legumes.

beginner: Chives planted around roses are a traditional pairing said to help keep aphids away and reduce black spot, and their early flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: A traditional aromatic-companion pairing: chives are long grown at the base of roses to deter aphids and reduce black spot, with allium sulfur volatiles the plausible mechanism. MSU relays it from Penn State as tradition, not a measured effect.

beginner: Chives grown at the base of an apple tree are traditionally said to help prevent apple scab.
seasoned: A traditional orchard pairing relayed by MSU (citing Penn State): chives ringing an apple trunk are said to help suppress apple scab. Folklore with an antifungal-allium rationale, not a documented trial.

beginner: Chives are in the onion family, which is toxic to cats and dogs (and horses), even though it is perfectly fine for people to eat. Keep the plants and any trimmings away from pets.
seasoned: Important safety note: chives are in the onion (allium) family, and all alliums are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses. They contain organosulfur compounds (N-propyl disulfide) that damage red blood cells and can cause hemolytic anemia, with cats the most sensitive, and raw, cooked, and dried parts are all toxic. Chives are safe for people in normal culinary amounts, but unlike a pet-safe herb such as rosemary, keep the plant and its trimmings away from pets. NC State lists Allium schoenoprasum as a problem for cats, dogs, and horses.

beginner: Keep chives and their clippings away from cats and dogs, and call a vet if your pet eats a lot.
seasoned: Grow chives where pets do not graze, and dispose of clippings where cats and dogs cannot reach them; if a pet eats a significant amount, contact a veterinarian.

seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), chives are a frost-hardy perennial, reliable to roughly zone 3. Establish a clump in spring after hard-frost danger, from a division or an indoor-started seedling, and it overwinters dormant and regrows early each spring. A single planting produces through the whole mild northern summer, since chives are cool-tolerant and not heat-stressed here, and holds into fall until hard frost. Shear low to keep leaves tender, shear the clump after flowering, and divide every 2 to 3 years.

beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, plant a chive clump once, from seed or a nursery division, in early spring around the last frost. Cut the leaves as they grow through spring; the clump slows and rests through the worst of the summer heat, then picks back up as the weather cools and is cut again into fall. Divide the clump every 2 to 3 years to keep it vigorous.
seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley grows chives as a hardy perennial planted once, in spring around the last frost, and cut repeatedly for years; the UNLV Master Gardener chart carries no chives-specific row, so this cell is modeled from the crop's own cool-preferring, cold-hardy perennial envelope and the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable framework (Fact Sheet FS-02-61). Once daytime highs push past the region's roughly 90°F growth ceiling from June into September, the clump slows, the leaves scorch, and cutting pauses; it resumes as the weather cools and the same clump is cut again through fall, then goes dormant over the mild winter. Divide the clump every 2 to 3 years to keep it vigorous. Zone 8's cooler pockets establish a little later in spring; zone 10 at Laughlin establishes earliest and its milder winter lets the fall cutting run a little longer.

beginner: Chives are one of the easiest and hardiest herbs you can grow. They are a perennial in the onion family, so you plant them once and they come back every year on their own. The plant dies back over winter, then sends up fresh, thin, grassy green leaves very early in spring, and it carries pretty pink-purple flowers in early summer that you can eat too. Chives like full sun to a little shade, decent soil, and regular water, but they forgive a lot. The clump gets bigger each year, so dig it up and split it every few years. They have a mild oniony taste and hardly any pests. There is also a relative called garlic chives, with flat leaves and a mild garlic flavor.
seasoned: Chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are a hardy, clump-forming perennial in the onion family (Amaryllidaceae), grown for their slender, hollow, grass-like leaves and their edible pink to pale purple pom-pom flowers. Unlike the annual and biennial kitchen herbs, chives are planted once and come back on their own year after year: the clump dies back to the ground over winter, rests dormant, and pushes up fresh green blades as one of the very first herbs of spring. They are among the hardiest herbs grown, reliable to roughly USDA zone 3, and among the easiest, with a mild onion flavor and few real pests. Give them full sun to light shade, average to rich well-drained soil, and steady moisture, though an established clump tolerates short dry spells. The clumps slowly widen from year to year and are best lifted and divided every 2 to 3 years to keep them vigorous. Chives are cool-preferring: in cold regions they run right through the northern summer, while in the hot South and desert they are a cool-season herb that slows or rests in the worst summer heat and revives as it cools. A close relative, garlic chives (Allium tuberosum), is a distinct species with flat leaves, a mild garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers.

beginner: You can start cutting chives once the clump is about 6 inches tall. From seed that takes a couple of months, but a bought or divided plant is ready much sooner. Snip the leaves down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil, taking some from each clump, and they grow right back so you can keep cutting all season. Always leave some green behind so the plant stays healthy, and go easy the first year. Cut in the cool morning and use the leaves fresh. The flowers are edible too.
seasoned: Start cutting chives once an established clump is 6 inches or more tall, which from seed is roughly 60 to 90 days but from a division or nursery clump can be just a few weeks. Harvest by shearing the outer leaves down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil with scissors, taking some blades from each clump rather than shearing it bare; the leaves regrow and you can cut the same plant again and again through the season. Leave enough green so the plant keeps feeding itself, and in the first year cut sparingly so the young clump can build strength to overwinter. Pick in the cool morning, and use the leaves fresh for the best flavor. The pink-purple flowers are edible too and are best picked just as they open.
